headline: DEA moves to deny medical cannabis firms in California, Illinois and 5 more
dek: DEA show-cause orders now reach California, Delaware, Illinois, North Dakota, Oregon and D.C., on top of Minnesota, citing dual licences and missing doctor sign-offs.
key_points: The DEA has sent orders to show cause to medical cannabis businesses in California, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Illinois, North Dakota and Oregon, Marijuana Moment reported on 11 November, adding to the Minnesota denial made public in late October.

The orders lean on two arguments: states that let the same businesses sell adult-use cannabis break the federal closed system, and states that let some patients buy without a written certification break the Single Convention's prescription rule.
MetaFlora's count of the DEA's own timely-applicant file dated 11 November shows 938 pending applications, including 613 dispensaries, in the six states and D.C. now facing these orders.
The registered side is pulling ahead: Trulieve says DEA registration ended its 280E tax burden, while a late-November supply-chain deadline will push timely applicants to trade only with each other.
body: The Drug Enforcement Administration has started telling medical cannabis businesses in some of the country's largest markets that it cannot register them under the federal rescheduling of state-licensed medical marijuana. Orders to show cause have gone to at least some applicants in California, Delaware, Illinois, North Dakota, Oregon and the District of Columbia, Marijuana Moment reported on 11 November, citing industry sources and the text of several orders. That comes on top of the Minnesota denial that became public at the end of October.

The orders are not final denials. They give a business a chance to respond, and the earlier Minnesota order offered a hearing request within 30 days or a corrective action plan. But the reasoning in them is about state law, not about any one company, which means the problem cannot be fixed by a better application. Until a state changes its rules, or the DEA changes its reading of them, operators in those states are on track to stay outside the federal Schedule III system that more than 900 dispensaries in seven medical-only states entered on 30 October.
## What the DEA is objecting to

Two arguments run through the orders, according to the documents Marijuana Moment reviewed. The first is the dual licence. Illinois, like Minnesota, lets businesses serve both medical patients and adult-use customers. The DEA's Illinois order says such a regime fails to provide robust protections against diversion, because non-medical use is still illegal under federal law, and that registering any applicant licensed under it would be inconsistent with the Controlled Substances Act and the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs.

The second is the missing paperwork. Federal rules adopted with rescheduling, at 21 CFR 1301.13(k), accept a state medical certification as the equivalent of a prescription only if it is signed and dated on the day it is issued and names the patient and a licensed practitioner. The DEA's California order says the state lets patients obtain an identification card on the basis of a note in their medical records, and that the state's written-documentation form is marked as optional. The Illinois order objects to the state's rule that lets veterans qualify with a year of VA medical records instead of a doctor's certification. The District of Columbia order, first reported by MJBizDaily, objects to patient self-certification.
> The DEA is not grading applications; it is grading state laws, and most of the country's medical cannabis is sold under laws it has now failed.

The DEA publishes a daily file of timely applicants, the businesses that filed complete applications between 28 April and 26 June and may keep operating under their state licences while they wait. MetaFlora counted the version dated 11 November. It lists 5,996 pending applications nationwide, including 3,211 dispensaries. In the six states and D.C. named in the new orders there are 938 pending applications: 771 in California, 82 in Illinois, 37 in Oregon, 30 in the District, 11 in North Dakota and 7 in Delaware. Of those, 613 are dispensaries. Minnesota adds another 30 applications, 26 of them dispensaries.

Not every one of those applicants has received an order, and the file does not name companies. But because the DEA's objections are to each state's rules, operators in those markets have little reason to expect a different outcome than their peers. A timely applicant whose application is finally denied loses the right to keep operating in the federal medical lane, according to the DEA's guidance on timely applicants.

The contrast with the seven states where registrations were granted, Alabama, Florida, Mississippi, South Dakota, Texas, Virginia and West Virginia, is sharpening. Trulieve, which now reports only its medical operations after deconsolidating Harvest's mixed medical and adult-use business in June, told investors on 5 November that rescheduling had brought DEA registration, the removal of the Section 280E tax penalty and its listing on the New York Stock Exchange. The company reported third-quarter revenue of $230 million and a 64% gross margin.

That is the prize that dual-licence operators are now further from. Section 280E bars businesses trafficking in Schedule I or II substances from deducting ordinary expenses; Schedule III businesses escape it. A Florida medical operator registered on 30 October and an Illinois operator facing a show-cause order may sell similar products, but they are now on different tax footing.

The DEA's own guidance adds a second squeeze. From late November, timely applicants and registrants may deal in Schedule III medical marijuana only with other timely applicants or registrants, and the agency says trading with anyone else could be grounds to deny an application or revoke a registration. If an applicant in a show-cause state is ultimately denied, its suppliers and customers in the federal lane would have to stop dealing with it.

States have choices, none of them quick. Minnesota's Office of Cannabis Management said after its denial that the DEA's order does not affect the state laws behind its medical and adult-use programs. States could split medical licences from adult-use ones, tighten certification rules so that each patient has a dated, signed practitioner document, or end self-certification and veteran shortcuts. Each change would need legislation or rulemaking, and some, such as the veteran pathway in Illinois, were deliberate policy choices.

The broader fix would come from the second half of rescheduling. A DEA administrative judge is considering whether to move non-medical marijuana to Schedule III too, after a hearing that concluded testimony earlier this autumn; no date for a recommendation has been announced. Even then, as Marijuana Moment has noted, adult-use sales involve no doctor's certification at all, so it is not clear how the agency's treaty reasoning would apply.

Responses to the orders are the first test. Businesses have 30 days to request a hearing or offer a corrective plan, so the first hearing requests from the late-October Minnesota order could surface in the coming weeks. Watch for state regulators in California, Illinois and Oregon to say whether they will change certification rules. The DEA's late-November supply-chain deadline will show how many businesses in the denied states drop out of the federal lane. And the administrative judge's recommendation on broader rescheduling remains the event that could change the map for every dual-licence state.
